title: 'You Can See Everything' Hits $19.5M, Surpasses 'Clayface' for Box Office #1 Spot
body:
The A24 documentary “You Can See Everything,” chronicling the rise and fall of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, captured the nation’s attention this weekend with a $19.5 million opening, eclipsing the debut of the superhero thriller “Clayface,” which earned $24 million but fell short of the documentary’s cultural buzz. The unexpected box‑office surge for the nonfiction film underscores a growing appetite for true‑crime storytelling, while also highlighting how streaming‑era audiences are still drawn to theatrical experiences that promise depth and relevance.

“​You Can See Everything” arrived in theaters after a limited‑run awards campaign and a high‑profile streaming release on a major platform. Its wide release, timed for the final weekend before the Academy Awards cut‑off, appears to have paid dividends. The documentary’s director, a former investigative journalist, blends archival footage, courtroom testimony, and exclusive interviews with former Theranos employees to paint a comprehensive portrait of one of the most infamous corporate frauds of the 21st century. Critics have praised its meticulous pacing and the way it humanizes both the charismatic founder and the victims of her deception, a balance that seems to have resonated with a broad demographic—from tech‑savvy millennials to older viewers who remember the headlines from the early 2010s.

Industry analysts point to several factors behind the film’s robust performance. First, the subject matter remains fresh in the public consciousness, thanks to recent high‑profile podcasts, a bestselling book, and a limited‑run series that kept the Theranos saga in the headlines. Second, the documentary’s release strategy—leveraging a brief streaming window before a theatrical rollout—generated a sense of urgency among viewers who feared missing out on the cultural conversation. Finally, the film’s modest budget, reportedly under $5 million, means the $19.5 million opening translates into a remarkable profit margin, reinforcing A24’s reputation for turning niche projects into box‑office hits.

“Clayface,” the latest entry from New York‑DC Studios, delivered a respectable $24 million opening, securing the top spot on the weekend’s box‑office chart. The R‑rated superhero thriller, starring a rising action star and directed by a veteran of genre cinema, appealed to core fans of gritty comic‑book adaptations. However, its performance also revealed the challenges faced by mid‑budget franchise entries in a market dominated by tentpole sequels and streaming releases. While “Clayface” benefited from a well‑timed release—coinciding with a weekend devoid of major studio blockbusters—its earnings fell short of the $30‑plus‑million benchmarks that similar films have achieved in recent years.

The contrast between the two films illustrates a shifting paradigm in theatrical economics. Audiences appear increasingly willing to trade popcorn for purpose, opting for documentaries that promise insight into real‑world events over conventional genre fare. This trend aligns with recent data showing a 12 percent rise in documentary attendance year‑over‑year, driven largely by titles that tackle high‑profile scandals or social issues. Studios are taking note; several major players have already green‑lit new nonfiction projects, betting that the formula of a compelling true‑story paired with strategic release windows can yield both critical acclaim and commercial success.

Looking ahead, “You Can See Everything” is poised to dominate the awards season conversation, with early buzz suggesting nominations in categories ranging from Best Documentary Feature to Best Editing. Its box‑office momentum may also encourage other distributors to experiment with hybrid release models that blend streaming accessibility with theatrical exclusivity. Meanwhile, “Clayface” will likely rely on international markets and ancillary revenue streams—home video, digital rentals, and merchandising—to recoup its investment and prove its viability as a franchise starter. As the industry navigates a post‑pandemic landscape, the weekend’s results underscore that compelling storytelling, whether factual or fictional, remains the ultimate driver of audience turnout.
